messages.body_plain:
I can't seem to post it as an attachment. Let's try this:

```
library(magrittr)
library(dplyr)
library(lavaan)

#' Okay, so, let's start with a basic 1-factor SEM/CFA off the iris data set. We're
#' going to set up a categorical variable but treat it as numeric to start. What
#' I'm expecting (and please correct me if this expectation is incorrect) is that
#' lavPredict could score the original training set of any SEM model and reproduce
#' the latent scores as if the entire training set was scored. And I start by
#' showing that this is true for the all-numeric case.
df <- iris %>%
mutate(species_fac = as.numeric(factor(Species))) %>%
select(-Species)

mdl <- sem(
'factor =~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width + species_fac'
, data = df
)
score_from_training <- lavPredict(mdl)[150,]

# The goal is to score a new record. We can't do that directly - Lavaan throws
# an error here even as numeric, species_fac has no variance.
lavPredict(mdl, newdata = df[150, ])

# One suggestion was to try appending new records to the original training set.
# This produces the EETAx error. For lavPredict, newdata cannot be larger than
# the original training set.
lavPredict(mdl, newdata = bind_rows(df, df[150, ]))

#okay so that's fine, I want to score just a single row. Let's artificially
#inject some variance by creating a synthetic row. We'll score both but keep
#only the actual data
synth <- data.frame(
Sepal.Length = 1
,Sepal.Width = 1
,Petal.Length = 1
,Petal.Width = 1
,species_fac = 1
) %>% bind_rows(df[150,])
possible_new_record <- lavPredict(mdl, newdata = synth)[2,]

# In the numeric case, this works. I get an exact match.
score_from_training == possible_new_record

# But this is not the case for the model with ordered observables.
mdl <- sem(
'factor =~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width + species_fac'
, data = df
, ordered = 'species_fac'
)

score_from_training <- lavPredict(mdl)[150,]
possible_new_record <- lavPredict(mdl, newdata = synth)[2,]

# Very different scores
score_from_training == possible_new_record
```

No, you are confusing the correlation among variables with the correlation among sample statistics (e.g., in samples with a higher loading for Item2, does Item3's loading also tend to be higher?).  That is not something for which you look at a variance-inflation factor.  You probably don't have to worry about that warning message, unless there is some other evidence that your model is not identified.  It is a warning, not an error.

messages.subject: [Lavaan 0.6-8 using R4.1.0] How are model parameters and degrees of freedom are counted when performing SEM with only manifest variables?
messages.subject_clean: [Lavaan 0.6-8 using R4.1.0] How are model parameters and degrees of freedom are counted when performing SEM with only manifest variables?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I've started recently a project where I have to perform mediation analysis using only manifest variables. As it goes on, I've come to realize I'm not so sure how model parameters and degrees of freedom are accounted for.

So, to make things simple, I took 5 numeric variables from my dataset and I have started to fit simple models and the result is i'm still confused. I'm not the biggest SEM expert there is, so I'm prepared to be educated, but still, I think I may have noticed some inconsistencies.

As a starter: I suppose we are ok that with 5 variables, I have (5*6)/2 = 15 unique variances/covariances to fit (I hope so, otherwise shoot me in the head already cause i'm so dumb...).

1/ A simple regression.
mod <- 'y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4'

fit <- sem(mod, data=test, estimator="ML")
summary(fit, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)

lavaan 0.6-8 ended normally after 13 iterations

  Estimator                                         ML
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of model parameters                         5

Model Test User Model:

  Test statistic                                 0.000
  Degrees of freedom                                 0

> parameterEstimates(fit)
   lhs op rhs    est    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
1    y  ~  x1  0.433 0.076  5.681  0.000    0.283    0.582
2    y  ~  x2  0.230 0.083  2.790  0.005    0.069    0.392
3    y  ~  x3  0.101 0.078  1.306  0.192   -0.051    0.253
4    y  ~  x4 -0.077 0.066 -1.168  0.243   -0.207    0.052
5    y ~~   y  6.460 0.670  9.644  0.000    5.147    7.772
6   x1 ~~  x1  7.930 0.000     NA     NA    7.930    7.930
7   x1 ~~  x2  3.224 0.000     NA     NA    3.224    3.224
8   x1 ~~  x3  1.645 0.000     NA     NA    1.645    1.645
9   x1 ~~  x4  3.277 0.000     NA     NA    3.277    3.277
10  x2 ~~  x2  7.573 0.000     NA     NA    7.573    7.573
11  x2 ~~  x3  3.539 0.000     NA     NA    3.539    3.539
12  x2 ~~  x4  2.433 0.000     NA     NA    2.433    2.433
13  x3 ~~  x3  7.563 0.000     NA     NA    7.563    7.563
14  x3 ~~  x4  2.258 0.000     NA     NA    2.258    2.258
15  x4 ~~  x4  9.676 0.000     NA     NA    9.676    9.676

So, I don't understand how the summary can say there are 5 model parameters, but there is 0 df (to me, it should be 15-5 = 10). All fit statistics such as RMSEA are at max/min value, so it seems the model is just identified according to lavaan but I think there is room for fitting more complex models than just a simple regression with 5 manifest variables. When looking at the parameterEstimates table, it seems all the covariances between exogenous variables are considered estimates, as well as variances. But estimates are fitted values according to the fitted.values(fit) matrix. Indeed, there are no SE, no test statistics, no CI95%. I've tried to fit the same model using the lm() function from base stat and regressions paremeters are estimated at the same value, so I suppose it's not the estimation that is the issue here (if there is any).

2/ Same model but putting all covariances between exogenous variables within the model formula
mod <- 'y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4

        x1 ~~ x2 + x3 + x4
        x2 ~~ x3 + x4
        x3 ~~ x4'

lavaan 0.6-8 ended normally after 59 iterations

  Estimator                                         ML
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of model parameters                        15

Model Test User Model:

  Test statistic                                 0.000
  Degrees of freedom                                 0

> parameterEstimates(fit)
   lhs op rhs    est    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
1    y  ~  x1  0.433 0.076  5.681  0.000    0.283    0.582
2    y  ~  x2  0.230 0.083  2.790  0.005    0.069    0.392
3    y  ~  x3  0.101 0.078  1.306  0.192   -0.051    0.253
4    y  ~  x4 -0.077 0.066 -1.168  0.243   -0.207    0.052
5   x1 ~~  x2  3.224 0.615  5.239  0.000    2.018    4.431
6   x1 ~~  x3  1.645 0.581  2.834  0.005    0.507    2.783
7   x1 ~~  x4  3.277 0.686  4.779  0.000    1.933    4.621
8   x2 ~~  x3  3.539 0.613  5.777  0.000    2.338    4.740
9   x2 ~~  x4  2.433 0.653  3.729  0.000    1.155    3.712
10  x3 ~~  x4  2.258 0.649  3.480  0.001    0.986    3.529
11   y ~~   y  6.460 0.670  9.644  0.000    5.147    7.772
12  x1 ~~  x1  7.930 0.822  9.644  0.000    6.319    9.542
13  x2 ~~  x2  7.573 0.785  9.644  0.000    6.034    9.112
14  x3 ~~  x3  7.563 0.784  9.644  0.000    6.026    9.100
15  x4 ~~  x4  9.676 1.003  9.644  0.000    7.709   11.642

So, in terms of parameter estimates, it seems it's the same model than before. So, when I saw those results, I was like "oh ok, by default, lavaan estimates covariances between all possible exogenous variables as model parameters". I've tried to mess with some lavaanOptions to see if I can understand but it was a failure. Also, the variances of those exogenous variables are also considered estimates. The paremeterEstimates table is quite close to the fist one but this time all columns are filled. Number of iterations is not in the same range than before... And, this is the really naive question, but should this model not be a 11 model parameters with 4 dfs (I don't understand why the variances of exogenous variables are considered parameters estimtes)? Also, maybe it's a wrong argument but I can fit a more complex model with more paths.

3/ A convoluted model
mod <- 'y ~ x3 + x4
        x2 ~ x1
        x3 ~ x2 + x1
        x4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3'

lavaan 0.6-8 ended normally after 19 iterations

  Estimator                                         ML
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of model parameters                        12

Model Test User Model:

  Test statistic                                49.355
  Degrees of freedom                                 2

> parameterEstimates(fit)
   lhs op rhs   est    se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
1    y  ~  x3 0.253 0.080 3.151  0.002    0.096    0.410
2    y  ~  x4 0.092 0.071 1.295  0.195   -0.047    0.231
3   x2  ~  x1 0.407 0.065 6.240  0.000    0.279    0.534
4   x3  ~  x2 0.458 0.071 6.436  0.000    0.319    0.598
5   x3  ~  x1 0.021 0.070 0.303  0.762   -0.115    0.157
6   x4  ~  x1 0.338 0.081 4.189  0.000    0.180    0.496
7   x4  ~  x2 0.093 0.091 1.014  0.311   -0.086    0.271
8   x4  ~  x3 0.182 0.085 2.138  0.032    0.015    0.348
9    y ~~   y 8.422 0.873 9.644  0.000    6.711   10.134
10  x2 ~~  x2 6.262 0.649 9.644  0.000    4.989    7.535
11  x3 ~~  x3 5.906 0.612 9.644  0.000    4.706    7.107
12  x4 ~~  x4 7.933 0.823 9.644  0.000    6.320    9.545
13  x1 ~~  x1 7.930 0.000    NA     NA    7.930    7.930

So, to me this model is indeed a 12 model parameters, but lavaan indicates there are only 2 dfs left. It seems the reason is lavaan considerd the variance of x1 (the only exogenous variable of the model) is a 13th estimate. As for the 1st model, it corresponds to the fitted value of the variance.

4/ Let's go crazy by saturating all the paths
mod <- 'y ~ x3 + x4
        x2 ~ x1
        x3 ~ x2 + x1
        x4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3

        x2 ~~ x3
        x2 ~~ x4
        x3 ~~ x4'

> fit <- sem(mod, data=test, estimator="ML")
Warning message:
In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.
> summary(fit, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)
lavaan 0.6-8 ended normally after 19 iterations

  Estimator                                         ML
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of model parameters                        15

Model Test User Model:

  Test statistic                                    NA
  Degrees of freedom                                -1

The model has 8 regressions paths, 4 residual variances, and 3 of them are correlated. So, there are indeed 15 model parameters, but as per lavaan, the model is underidentified.
> parameterEstimates(fit)
   lhs op rhs   est se  z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
1    y  ~  x3 0.253 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
2    y  ~  x4 0.092 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
3   x2  ~  x1 0.407 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
4   x3  ~  x2 0.438 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
5   x3  ~  x1 0.029 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
6   x4  ~  x1 0.340 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
7   x4  ~  x2 0.093 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
8   x4  ~  x3 0.170 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
9   x2 ~~  x3 0.128 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
10  x2 ~~  x4 0.029 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
11  x3 ~~  x4 0.070 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
12   y ~~   y 8.422 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
13  x2 ~~  x2 6.262 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
14  x3 ~~  x3 5.909 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
15  x4 ~~  x4 7.934 NA NA     NA       NA       NA
16  x1 ~~  x1 7.930  0 NA     NA     7.93     7.93

Again, the variance of x1, the only exogenous variable of the model is considered an estimate.

5/ Let's fit a 5 model parameters by specyfing constraints on the model formula: no covariances between exogenous variables
mod <- 'y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4

        x1 ~~ 0*x2 + 0*x3 + 0*x4
        x2 ~~ 0*x3 + 0*x4
        x3 ~~ 0*x4'

lavaan 0.6-8 ended normally after 14 iterations

  Estimator                                         ML
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of model parameters                         9

Model Test User Model:

  Test statistic                               118.287
  Degrees of freedom                                 6

> parameterEstimates(fit)
   lhs op rhs    est    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
1    y  ~  x1  0.433 0.066  6.537  0.000    0.303    0.562
2    y  ~  x2  0.230 0.068  3.402  0.001    0.098    0.363
3    y  ~  x3  0.101 0.068  1.496  0.135   -0.031    0.234
4    y  ~  x4 -0.077 0.060 -1.290  0.197   -0.195    0.040
5   x1 ~~  x2  0.000 0.000     NA     NA    0.000    0.000
6   x1 ~~  x3  0.000 0.000     NA     NA    0.000    0.000
7   x1 ~~  x4  0.000 0.000     NA     NA    0.000    0.000
8   x2 ~~  x3  0.000 0.000     NA     NA    0.000    0.000
9   x2 ~~  x4  0.000 0.000     NA     NA    0.000    0.000
10  x3 ~~  x4  0.000 0.000     NA     NA    0.000    0.000
11   y ~~   y  6.460 0.670  9.644  0.000    5.147    7.772
12  x1 ~~  x1  7.930 0.822  9.644  0.000    6.319    9.542
13  x2 ~~  x2  7.573 0.785  9.644  0.000    6.034    9.112
14  x3 ~~  x3  7.563 0.784  9.644  0.000    6.026    9.100
15  x4 ~~  x4  9.676 1.003  9.644  0.000    7.709   11.642

It's the same model than 1 and 2. Estimates of regression paths are the same. This time : 9 model parameters + 6 dfs = 15. But, should it not be a 5 model parameters?

6/ Let's take the simplest model and specify just one covariance between two exogenous variables
mod <- 'y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4

        x1 ~~ x2'

fit <- sem(mod, data=test, estimator="ML")
Warning message:
In lav_partable_vnames(FLAT, "ov.x", warn = TRUE) : lavaan WARNING:
    model syntax contains variance/covariance/intercept formulas
    involving (an) exogenous variable(s): [x1 x2]; These variables
    will now be treated as random introducing additional free
    parameters. If you wish to treat those variables as fixed, remove
    these formulas from the model syntax. Otherwise, consider adding
    the fixed.x = FALSE option.
> summary(fit, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)
lavaan 0.6-8 ended normally after 21 iterations

  Estimator                                         ML
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of model parameters                         8

Model Test User Model:

  Test statistic                                69.501
  Degrees of freedom                                 4

So, when I have added all covariances (second example), no warnings, but If i add just one there is an issue. And now, it's a 8 model parameters with 4 dfs.

7/To conclude, I have fitted a one factor CFA with the 4 Xs variables as indicators and the results were crystal clear to me.

In the end, I can really contemplate the possibility I'm stupid. If so, please educate me, I will be thankful. But at the very least, I think there is maybe something a little bit confusing here.

Kind regards,
Antoine Vanier

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
So, I did my homework. Turns out the main issue is the fact that I was so used to fit tons on CFA models with latent variables I became puzzled the moment I had to fit a path analysis.

Anyway, I've found a nice website page about the issue : https://fredclavel.org/2014/05/03/disentangling-degrees-of-freedom-for-sem/ .

I' ve read it and I did hand calculations of df for the tested model and the baseline model of all the examples I have tried above and I figured it out. It's cool, I have learned a lot about df and model parameters count in SEM.
To conclude, you can call me stupid. Sorry for the inconvenience. At the very least, I'm a little less stupid now and for others who are confused with this topic, you can check out the link above.

Have a nice day all.
Antoine Vanier

messages.subject: Function for bootstrapped confidence intervals of standardized solution?
messages.subject_clean: Function for bootstrapped confidence intervals of standardized solution?
messages.body_plain:
Hi lavaan group,

I was wondering if `lavaan` or `semTools` has created a function for automating bootstrapped confidence intervals for the standardized solution from SEM models estimated using `lavaan`. I noticed the standardizedSolution() function does not have a `boot.ci.type` argument like the parameterEstimates() function does. The standardizedSolution() help page does not mention bootstrapped confidence intervals and says if the `ci` argument is TRUE, that "simple symmetric confidence intervals are added to the output". Thus, while the standardizedSolution() function can provide confidence intervals of the standardized solution, I assume this means it can not provide bootstrapped confidence intervals.

I noticed there is a post from 2014 that shows a way to do this using the bootstrapLavaan() function: https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/pIXy7NUa3c0/m/hVPH3zClaYcJ. However, it has been 7 years since then and I was wondering if lavaan, semTools, or any other R package has created a function for automating the calculation of bootstrapped confidence intervals of the standardized solution?

If not, I guess you could treat this post as a feature request. I think this would be of interest to a lot of users as social science researchers are more and more interested in having 1) more interpretable (e.g., standardized) effect sizes, 2) confidence intervals around those effect sizes, 3) robust versions (e.g., bootstrapping) of such confidence intervals.

Best,
-David

messages.subject: Re: Inconsistant pvalue in parameterEstimates and standardizedSolutions
messages.subject_clean: Inconsistant pvalue in parameterEstimates and standardizedSolutions
messages.body_plain:
Rebekka,

This comes up now and again. It applies to regression in general, not just SEM or lavaan.

The parameter estimate is a single estimate with uncertainty.

The standardized parameter estimate transforms that with a calculation that uses two other estimates (the variances), each with their own uncertainty.

So you shouldn't expect the p-values to be the same. Always draw conclusions based on the unstandardized estimate and its tests/CIs. Standardized estimates are nothing more than a convenience for interpretation.

Pat

If by 'control variable' you mean something analogous to a covariate in ANCOVA, the usual way is to regress all your model variables on it.

So

X ~ C
M1 ~ a*X + C
etc.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: GOF indices for a probit model with ordinal covariates in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: GOF indices for a probit model with ordinal covariates in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Carlos,

Two things.

1) In SEM, exogenous variables are treated as interval, even if they are not continuous. That is why lavaan rejects declaring them as categorical. This is generally fine for continuous and binary variables, but not for multi-category discrete variables, whether ordinal or nominal. For those, you need to create dummy or effect codes.

2) For your other question, your model is saturated and necessarily fits perfectly. So you are getting fit measures, but they look odd because there are no degrees of freedom that would you give you basis to reject the model.

As a side note, regression procedures outside SEM almost always use saturated models. Since your model is a univariate multiple regression, your results should be parallel to those of glm (aside from differences introduced by the estimator or missing data handling).

Pat

Dear Pat,

Thank you very much for your attention and prompt reply.

About 1), I thought that “lavaan” was handling the ordinal covariates correctly because the program issued a warning and not an error message.

In the “lavaan” model, the variance and intercept of the response variable are both fixed. “lavaan” works from the variance-covariance matrix, which is different from “glm”.

I want to compare this basic probit regression model with both "glm" and one or two SEM based on the same variables, to see whether the SEMs provide evidence on the plausibility of the causal hypotheses embodied in them. For this, I need a lavaan probit model that yields measures of overall misfit.

I will try your suggestion of generating dummy variables for the ordinal covariates, testing first with one or two variables, and see if this change leads to a model that is not saturated.

Once again, many thanks for your time and attention,

Carlos M. Lemos

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Laura.

1. Looks reasonable.

2. Generally speaking, if you're relying on fit indices, you want all the major ones to be good. What are you chi-squared and df? Most often, the pattern you're seeing happens when variables have low correlations in the data. CFI compares the fit of your model to a null model. If the null model (assumes everything uncorrelated) isn't too bad, then CFI will be bad.

But you should probe to see where the misfit is coming from. The most likely source in your model is where one or more covariates are more closely related to some of your x variables than to the others. Start by looking at lavResiduals()  and focusing on those relations.

3. cluster="city" (and take out the city dummies)

Hope this helps,
Pat

messages.body_plain:
Carlos,

Since your lavaan model as specified is a generalized linear multiple regression, the only way to introduce misfit would be to constrain one or more of the regression coefficients. This seems pretty arbitrary.

And getting a deviance statistic from glm() does not mean the model is not saturated. You didn't share your glm() function call, but unless you went out of your way (such as my previous paragraph), it is saturated. If you ask for fit measures from lavaan, you'll also see -2LL, AIC, etc., even from a saturated model.

Pat

>

> For clustering SE, I thought the only possible way is to use the survey lavaan package? And when using the cluster = "city" option in the sem(), can i still have the cities in the regression as I intend them to have as like fixed effects?
lavaan.survey has not been updated since 2016. The cluster= argument in lavaan() is now preferred. Using the city dummies adjusts only means/intercepts. Using cluster="city" also handles partitioning of variance. But look into resources on centering options for multilevel regression--the same logic will carry into lavaan.

>  Also when running the survey lavaan package , clustered_STS <-svydesign(ids=~city, data=data) and lavaan.survey(results, clustered_STS) from results <- sem(model, data=data, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE), compared to the cluster-option,results <- sem(model, data=data, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, cluster="city") I received "Robust.cluster.sem", with information =Expected and Information saturated (h1) model = Structures  vs. "Robust.cluster" for the cluster option, information=observed and observed information based on =Hessian. What exactly are those differences?
I've never used lavaan.survey -- can't speak to this.

> I am detecting weird movements in the CFI. As I only have one observation in 6 cities, I have put them together in one "city" so that the variance is not zero. However, by doing so, the CFI decreases massively. Also when I take out those 6 observations and the city dummies from the regression, the CFI is low again (df=233,chisq= 710.441). However, if I individually add the cities with only one individual as dummies into the regression, the CFI is high (0.95 with df=257, chisquar =  736.838 as N=4868). What is happening here ?
There's no need to do this. Clusters can be of size 1 (if all clusters are size 1, you'll get exactly the same results as a non-clustered model).

> Also I always (for any city combination) receive the following warnings: Warning message:In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :lavaan WARNING:The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue (= -2.960830e-16) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that  the model is not identified. - I have read that this could be a numerical issue. Can I just ignore this warning?
This question is asked frequently on this list. The general advice is that if the solution is reasonable, you can probably disregard.

Pat

Dear Pat,

Thank you very much for your time and patience in hanging on and helping me!

Here is the call to “glm” (I used probit link so that the results could be more closely compared with those by “lavaan”):

> fit <- glm(model, family = binomial(link = "probit"), data = na.omit(df))

The formula is as follows, with the same data frame and variables:

> fit$formula

[1] "CHG.UNAFFILIATED  ~  CHG.UNBELIEVER + CONFIDENCE.CHURCHES + POWER.CHURCHES + REL.RELEVANCE.TODAY + REL.REPRESENTS.PAST + NUM.UNAFFILIATED.PARENTS + ATTEND.11.12 + SEX + AGE.GROUP + DEGREE + HHCHILDR + URBRURAL"

The model computed by “glm” has 28 parameters

> fit$rank

[1] 28

and is not saturated because

> fit$df.residual

[1] 703

i.e. there are a lot more data points than coefficients (parameters) to be estimated. With this, I can get several GOF indices, for example:

> with(fit,c(deviance,aic))

[1] 559.2648 615.2648

Returning to “lavaan”, I inspected the solution (also named "fit") in my first post:

> fitted(fit)

and found that the only free parameters are the threshold of the response variable and the regression coefficients. You're welcome.

And if it helps, df means something completely different in the two analyses. df in SEM packages doesn't depend on N. And as I said, you can get things like AIC from a saturated model in lavaan by asking for fit measures. D and AIC are not measures of absolute fit--you can't reject a model with them. They're only useful for relative fit.

Pat

In the “lavaan” model, the variance and intercept of the response variable are both fixed. “lavaan” works from the variance-covariance matrix, which is different from “glm”.

messages.subject_clean: Help with checking if SEM model is correct
messages.body_plain:
Hi there -

I am running an analysis which considers the role of conspiracy theories  and its relationship between stress and anxiety - and controlling for Social status, age, education and political orientation.

I am tying to get the model correct before I collect data - so I can pre-register the code

However - I am having trouble with coding it correctly (I think) and would be interested if anyone has any tips for this.

require(lavaan)
require(semPlot)

#model syntax
SEM_mod <- '
#Measurement model
Conspiracy =~ BCT1 + BCT2 + BCT3 + BCT4 + BCT5 + BCT6 + BCT7 + BCT8 + BCT9 + BCT10 + BCT11 + BCT12 + BCT13 + BCT14 + BCT15
Stress =~ PSS1 + PSS2 + PSS3 + PSS4 + PSS5 + PSS6 + PSS7 + PSS8 + PSS9 + PSS10
Anxiety =~ GAD1 + GAD2 + GAD3 + GAD4 + GAD5 + GAD6 + GAD7
#Regressions
Conspiracy ~ Stress + Anxiety + SSocial + Age + Ed + Political
Anxiety + Stress ~~ SSocial + Age + Ed + Political
SSocial ~~ Age + Ed + Political
Age ~~ Ed + Political
Political ~~ Ed
'
#Estimate model
fit = sem(SEM_mod)
ordered(TRUE)

#generate model
semPaths(fit,
nCharNodes = 0, #disable abbreviates if set to 0
sizeMan = 3, # size of manifest variables
sizeLat = 8, # size of latent variables
rotation = 2, #rotates the plot
layout = 'tree2', # tree layout options
curve = 1.5, #curve of correlation lines
)

messages.subject_clean: Help with checking if SEM model is correct
messages.body_plain:
Nick,

Registering the code before you collect data is great. But if you want to do so, the best way to test your code is to simulate data. Look into simsem. You don't need to do a full-blown simulation, but you need a plausible dataset (preferably with some missingness).

Also, there's no need for the ~~ lines. It appears your structural model is essentially a multiple regression, and the exogenous variables will freely covary using the sem() call. If you do 'bring them into the model" this way, you may need to add Anxiety ~~ Stress.

Pat

messages.body_plain:
Laura,

For point 1, I'm not sure.

For point 2, no, you shouldn't expect the same results. A factor is latent--it is definitionally something different that you can get from the manifest variables. A weighted mean will include (possibly systematic) error. It also doesn't account for imprecision in the estimates of the factor loadings. Finally, factor loadings aren't weights.

If you want observed variables that best reflect the factor, look into the plausible values literature--I can't recall off hand whether it's lavaan or semTools that can generate these, but one of them can.

Pat
